blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. In a controlled evaluation that fixes the candidate pool, verifier, and budget and employs reference-annotated degradation states, PreActIR uses 42.5% fewer real tool calls and 63.4% fewer rejected calls than reactive, execute-then-evaluate trial and error, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Image restoration has advanced rapidly for individual degradations
such as noise, blur, rain, haze, low light, compression, and low resolution ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2018a ; Wei et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Zamir et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Zamir et al., 2021 ; Zamir et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Liang et al., 2021 ; Tu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) . In practice, however, several degradations often coexist and
interact, making restoration a sequential decision problem in which each
intervention changes both the image state and the value of later actions.
Recent agentic systems coordinate specialized tools through
perception, planning, execution, and feedback ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Zuo et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) .
Most of them follow an execute–observe–replan loop ( Yao et al., 2023 ) :
a tool’s effect on a given image is known only after it has run, failed calls
still cost computation, and harmful side effects go unnoticed until
afterwards.

blocks.en:
Recent agents reduce the number of trials with trained planners and stored
experience ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ,
and a few methods score actions in advance: DiTTo ( Choi and Oh, 2026 ) learns a
simulator and a per-action quality predictor for trajectory construction, and
the concurrent Causal-AgentIR ( Gao et al., 2026 ) estimates plan
utility from a causal memory of past executions. Neither trains a
tool-conditioned consequence model for deployment-time decisions. A separate
question is whether the tool set itself is the limit: even a perfect selector fails if no reachable
tool sequence yields a good result. Agents can add experts ( Choi and Oh, 2026 ) or fine-tune tools together with the planner ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) , but a poor
result alone does not tell whether the selector chose badly or no good
candidate was reachable—two cases that call for different fixes. As
illustrated in Fig. 1 , reactive execution pays for an
outcome before seeing it, and it is usually unclear whether the selector or the
tool set is the binding limit.

blocks.en:
We propose PreActIR , an agentic restoration framework built around
the idea that an agent should predict what a tool will do before calling it.
A tool-conditioned world model takes each candidate tool and predicts the
changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, along with
content damage, the probabilities of benefit and harm, and the uncertainty of
these predictions. The agent ranks candidates by these predictions and
executes only the top one. Because predictions can be wrong, an independent
post-execution verifier checks the actual output and commits or rolls it
back; the agent then replans from the observed state. We call this the
predict–act–verify loop.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are as follows: • A tool-conditioned world model that predicts how each
candidate tool changes residual degradation, quality, and fidelity, along
with benefit and harm probabilities and uncertainty, so
that tools can be ranked and their risk estimated before execution. • A predict–act–verify loop that executes only the
top-ranked tool and lets an independent verifier commit or roll back its
output; in a matched replay with reference-annotated states, it makes
42.5% fewer real calls and 63.4% fewer rejections than reactive
trial and error. • A candidate-frontier audit that distinguishes tool-selection limitations from candidate-space constraints by characterizing attainable fidelity–perception trade-offs. It quantifies the headroom available through better selection within a fixed pool and examines how targeted tool adaptation expands the attainable frontier.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
All-in-one image restoration addresses multiple degradations within a unified
model using degradation-aware representations, multimodal guidance, or adaptive
expert routing ( Li et al., 2022 ; Potlapalli et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Conde et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Zamfir et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
These methods learn a fixed policy without predicting tool effects before
execution. Agentic restoration instead coordinates specialized models through
perception, planning, execution, and feedback, building on
reinforcement-learned toolchains ( Yu et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) .
MLLM controllers reason about degradations and coordinate
experts ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) ;
AgenticIR, MAIR, 4KAgent, SEAR, HybridAgent, and FAPE-IR add exploration
with rollback, multi-agent or recursive execution, tree search, fast–slow
coordination, and frequency-aware planning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) ;
and others target rain, inscriptions, or photo
retouching ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026b ; Xiong et al., 2026 ) .
In these systems a tool’s effect is observed only after it runs, and SEAR’s
tree search scores candidates by real rollouts.

blocks.en:
Restore-R1, TIR-Agent, and OPERA train the planner with perceptual or metric
rewards ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026a ) , and OPERA also
fine-tunes the tools; SkillIR reuses skills from past
executions ( Shao et al., 2026 ) , and PaAgent retrieves tool-specific experience
from a portrait bank of restoration tools ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . These methods improve the choice of tool but do not predict what it will do. DiTTo ( Choi and Oh, 2026 ) learns a
restoration simulator and a per-action quality predictor, but uses them to
build order-aware training trajectories. The concurrent
Causal-AgentIR ( Gao et al., 2026 ) keeps a causal memory graph of past
executions, curated by a learned memory-operation policy, and scores plans
before execution by multi-hop reasoning over retrieved memory paths, with a
critic and rollback afterwards. Pre-execution scoring and rollback are therefore
not new on their own. PreActIR differs in that it trains a consequence
model on real transitions and queries it for every candidate at
deployment time, predicting separate outcomes rather than collapsing them into
a single score; it also audits whether the selector or the tool set limits performance.

blocks.en:
World models learn action-conditioned dynamics so that an agent can evaluate
actions in imagination before acting ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ) .
Probabilistic models quantify their own uncertainty ( Chua et al., 2018 ) ,
short rollouts limit compounding model error ( Janner et al., 2019 ) , and a
model need not reconstruct observations if it predicts only decision-relevant
quantities ( Schrittwieser et al., 2020 ) . Among language agents, PreAct
predicts action results before acting ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , and WebDreamer
uses an LLM to simulate each candidate web action before choosing
one ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . Those predictions are free-form text from a
pretrained model, whereas restoration tool outcomes are continuous and
multi-dimensional, and fidelity to the unknown clean image is unobservable at
test time. Our consequence heads are instead supervised with uncertainty
estimates on real tool transitions; we plan one step ahead by default and rely on a
post-execution verifier to catch the remaining prediction errors.

blocks.en: 3.2 Overview
blocks.zh: 3.2 概览

blocks.en:
PreActIR follows a predict–act–verify loop (Fig. 2 ). A
tool-conditioned world model predicts structured action consequences before
execution (Sec. 3.3 ), and an independent verifier commits or
rolls back each executed action (Sec. 3.4 ). An offline
candidate-frontier audit then checks whether the candidate space limits
performance, and targeted tool adaptation is studied as a controlled way to
expand it (Sec. 3.5 ).

blocks.en: 4.1 Datasets and Experimental Setup
blocks.zh: 4.1 数据集和实验设置

blocks.en:
PreActIR is evaluated on MiO100 ( Kong et al., 2024 ) under the AgenticIR
protocol ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , with 160 official compound-degradation states from
20 clean-image identities for training and 1,440 test images across
Groups A–C. We use five-fold cross-fitting with disjoint clean-image
identities between fitting and outer validation. The
base tool set 𝒜 \mathcal{A} contains 33 restoration actions covering eight
degradation types. Sec. 4.2 (Tables 1 – 2 ) reports the full system, in
which the world model pre-ranks root actions, only high-value roots are
executed and expanded, and cross-fitted candidate-value models select the
output, with a fixed output blend for Groups A and B (Appendix C ).
For Group C, it also includes a HAT-S operator ( Chen et al., 2023 ) adapted on
4,000 external degradation-matched pairs, without MiO100 HQ images or test
references (Appendix G ). Controlled planner
comparisons (Secs. 4.3 – 4.4 ) use
matched candidate pools and tool sets.

blocks.en: 4.4 Predict-before-Act versus Reactive Trial-and-Error
blocks.zh: 4.4 诉讼前预测与反演审判和反演

blocks.en:
The previous section evaluated ranking from frozen outcomes; here we test
whether better ranking saves real tool calls when failures
are costly. In a controlled replay on the same 160 OOF states, three policies
share the candidate pool, an annotated degradation state, the post-execution
verifier, and a budget of four real calls; each executes candidates in its
own order, rolls back rejected outputs, and stops at the first verified one.
The pool contains the 1,415 candidates executed when constructing the training
transitions: all tools for each state’s annotated degradation types, plus up
to two randomly drawn tools from other types (7–12 per state). Because the shared
state uses annotated degradation types and severities computed
from the clean reference, the replay isolates execution order under an
accurate state rather than estimating deployment performance
(Sec. 4.3 ). Reactive
trial-and-error orders targets by presence times severity (floored at 0.05) and tools by a
per-target route fitted on two inner identities; fidelity-head ranking (WM-F) and
PreActIR order the same candidates by predicted fidelity gain v v and by
structured utility U t U_{t} , respectively. With the verifier threshold fixed per fold,
only the ordering differs.

blocks.en: 4.5 Candidate-Frontier Audit and Targeted Tool Adaptation
blocks.zh: 4.5 候选人-前沿审计和定向工具调整

blocks.en:
No amount of better prediction helps if no reachable candidate is good enough.
We therefore audit whether Group C is limited by selection or by what the
33-action tool set can produce. Using test references post hoc, we score all 21,385
frozen Group C candidates and solve an exact one-candidate-per-state
mixed-integer program that maximizes mean Y-PSNR subject to a floor on mean
MUSIQ; sweeping the floor traces the attainable fidelity–perception frontier
of the fixed pool (Fig. 7 a). This oracle is not
deployable, but it shows where the ceiling is. The deployed fixed-pool
configuration lies well inside the frontier: at its MUSIQ level, a
reference-assisted selection from the same pool reaches 21.74
versus 19.97 dB Y-PSNR, leaving 1.77 dB
of selector headroom. Adapting HAT-S on 4,000 external replay pairs
expands the pool for the 200 low-resolution states and raises the attainable
frontier by 0.50 dB at the final MUSIQ level. Our final Group C system builds
on a different fixed-pool configuration and fuses the adapted tool’s output
into the low-resolution states; it reaches 21.05/0.604 Y-PSNR/Y-SSIM at MUSIQ
54.78 but still lies 0.7 dB below the fixed-pool frontier. On the two
low-resolution combinations it exceeds the fixed-pool oracle, while the
other two retain 1.6–2.6 dB of selector headroom
(Fig. 7 b). Tool adaptation is one practical route to a better operating point, but closing the selector
headroom offers a larger gain.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that looks before it
restores: a tool-conditioned world model predicts the consequences of each
candidate tool before execution, and an independent verifier commits or rolls
back the executed one. In controlled replays with matched candidates, verifier,
and budget, predicting before acting substantially reduces real and rejected
tool calls while improving restoration quality, and on MiO100 the full system
achieves the best overall performance on all three compound-degradation groups.
The candidate-frontier audit shows where the remaining gains lie: the
existing tool set holds considerable headroom for better selection, and
targeted adaptation can push the frontier further. Two directions remain
open: validating these gains under estimated degradation states and
establishing whether multi-step imagination adds value beyond single-step
ranking.
